                                                                                       Clearly Established Law)

                                                                                       JURY TRIAL DEMANDED
_____________________________________________________________
INTRODUCTION
1. This is a civil rights action under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 arising from an unconstitutional administrative proceeding that destroyed Plaintiff’s livelihood. Plaintiff Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi (“Plaintiff”) brings this First Amended Complaint against two defendants: (1) Diana Candelaria (“Candelaria”), a Driver Safety Hearing Officer employed by the California Department of Motor Vehicles (“DMV”), sued in her individual capacity for compensatory and punitive damages; and (2) Steve Gordon (“Director Gordon”), Director of the California Department of Motor Vehicles, sued in his official capacity for declaratory and injunctive relief pursuant to the Ex parte Young doctrine, 209 U.S. 123 (1908).
2. The administrative record in this case strips the controversy of any ambiguity and reduces it to a single, inescapable conclusion: the State of California, acting through Defendant Candelaria, destroyed a man’s livelihood based on an arrest that the arresting agency itself formally repudiated, through a hearing that ignored binding precedent and objective evidence, and before a decisionmaker who functioned as a prosecutor rather than a judge.
3. The undisputed chronology is as follows:
On November 1, 2024, Plaintiff was lawfully parked on an unpaved dirt shoulder, asleep in a stationary vehicle. He had made the responsible decision to rest rather than drive while fatigued—exactly what his commercial driver training instructed. California Highway Patrol (“CHP”) officers approached under the guise of a “welfare check,” but within fourteen seconds of arrival—before conducting any welfare assessment—one officer declared “I think it’s booze,” revealing an immediate criminal investigative motive. The officers then conducted a warrantless entry and search of Plaintiff’s vehicle while he remained asleep, and arrested him for DUI despite never observing him drive.
On November 5, 2024—eleven weeks before the DMV hearing—the arresting agency itself issued a formal Detention Certificate under California Penal Code § 849(b)(1), certifying that there were “insufficient grounds” for prosecution and that, by operation of state law, the encounter “shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention only.” No criminal charges were ever filed.
On January 24, 2025, Defendant Candelaria presided over Plaintiff’s Administrative Per Se (“APS”) hearing. Plaintiff presented the Detention Certificate, the CHP dashcam video transcript, and binding California Supreme Court precedent (Mercer v. DMV) establishing that the warrantless arrest was unlawful. Candelaria dismissed every defense as “unpersuasive” without reasoned analysis, failed entirely to address the Detention Certificate—the single most dispositive piece of evidence in the proceeding—applied an irrebuttable presumption of official regularity to override objective contrary evidence, and issued a decision that reads as a defense of the officers’ actions rather than a neutral evaluation of the facts.
On February 11, 2025, Candelaria issued a written Notification of Findings and Decision sustaining a one-year suspension of Plaintiff’s driving privileges, effectively disqualifying his Class A Commercial Driver’s License (“CDL”) from February 20, 2025 through February 19, 2026, and imposing a $125.00 reissue fee and a three-year SR-22 proof of financial responsibility requirement.
4. The APS implied consent framework under California Vehicle Code §§ 13353 and 13353.2 requires as a jurisdictional predicate that the driver was “lawfully arrested.” When the arresting agency itself has formally certified that the arrest lacked sufficient grounds and is legally reclassified as a detention only, the “lawful arrest” predicate ceases to exist as a matter of law. Defendant Candelaria proceeded anyway—exercising adjudicative power over a subject matter that, by the State’s own formal admission, did not exist.
5. Compounding this jurisdictional nullity, Defendant Candelaria operated within a structurally biased framework squarely condemned by the California Court of Appeal in California DUI Lawyers Ass’n v. DMV (2022) 77 Cal.App.5th 517 and Knudsen v. DMV (2024) 101 Cal.App.5th 186—serving simultaneously as the prosecuting advocate for the DMV and the ostensible adjudicator of fact. Her decision reflects not neutral judgment but advocacy for a predetermined outcome.
6. This deprivation is not merely historical. Plaintiff’s CDL remains suspended. Each day the suspension continues, Plaintiff is barred from his profession, denied his primary source of income, and subjected to an ongoing constitutional violation. This continuing deprivation entitles Plaintiff to prospective injunctive and declaratory relief against Director Gordon under the Ex parte Young doctrine.
7. The systemic implications of this case extend far beyond Plaintiff’s individual suspension. The structural defects at issue—the dual advocate-adjudicator framework and the DMV’s practice of sustaining license suspensions based on arrests that have been formally nullified by the arresting agency’s own Detention Certificates—are not unique to this case. They are features of a statewide administrative system operating under Director Gordon’s supervision. A federal ruling that the DMV cannot suspend a driver’s license when the arrest predicate has been statutorily erased could affect every APS case involving a Penal Code § 849(b)(1) release.
JURISDICTION AND VENUE
8. This Court has original subject-matter jurisdiction pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1331 (federal question) and 28 U.S.C. § 1343(a)(3) and (4) (civil rights) because this action arises under the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution and 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
9. Venue is proper in this District under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(1) and (2) because Defendant Candelaria is employed by the DMV within this District, Defendant Gordon maintains his principal office in Sacramento within this District, and a substantial part of the events giving rise to this action occurred within the Eastern District of California.
10. Plaintiff’s claim for declaratory and injunctive relief against Defendant Gordon in his official capacity is authorized by the Ex parte Young doctrine, Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908), which permits suit against a state official in official capacity for prospective relief to halt ongoing violations of federal law. The Eleventh Amendment does not bar this claim.
PARTIES
11. Plaintiff BRENDAN NGEHSI NEWANFORBI is an individual residing in Stockton, San Joaquin County, California. At all relevant times, Plaintiff held a valid California Class A CDL and was employed as a professional commercial truck driver by Centerline Drivers, LLC, assigned to the Lily Transportation—Toyota Dedicated route in San Ramon, California, earning a regular hourly rate of $33.35 and premium rate of $50.03, with a start date of October 30, 2024—just two days before the encounter that gave rise to this action.
12. Defendant DIANA CANDELARIA is, and at all relevant times was, employed by the California Department of Motor Vehicles as a Driver Safety Hearing Officer within the Legal Affairs Division, Driver Safety Branch. Candelaria presided over Plaintiff’s APS hearing held remotely via Microsoft Teams on January 24, 2025, and issued a written Notification of Findings and Decision dated February 11, 2025, in APS Case No. 34739340. Candelaria is sued exclusively in her individual capacity for compensatory and punitive damages.
13. At all times relevant hereto, Defendant Candelaria acted under color of the statutes, regulations, customs, and usages of the State of California, and within the course and scope of her employment with the DMV, clothed with the authority of state law.
14. Defendant STEVE GORDON is the Director of the California Department of Motor Vehicles. Director Gordon is responsible for the administration and enforcement of the DMV’s statewide policies, procedures, and operations, including the APS hearing framework under which Plaintiff’s license was suspended. Director Gordon is sued exclusively in his official capacity for prospective declaratory and injunctive relief pursuant to the Ex parte Young doctrine. No monetary damages are sought against Director Gordon.
STATEMENT OF FACTS
A. Plaintiff’s Protected Property Interest
15. At all relevant times, Plaintiff held a valid California Class A CDL, which constituted a protected property interest under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Bell v. Burson, 402 U.S. 535, 539 (1971) (“[L]icenses are not to be taken away without that procedural due process required by the Fourteenth Amendment.”); Mackey v. Montrym, 443 U.S. 1, 10–11 (1979).
16. Plaintiff’s CDL was not merely a personal convenience; it was the indispensable foundation of his professional livelihood. As a commercial truck driver, the CDL was a mandatory prerequisite for his employment. Its suspension immediately and completely extinguished his capacity to earn a living in his chosen profession.
17. On October 30, 2024—just two days before the encounter that precipitated this action—Plaintiff commenced active employment with Centerline Drivers, LLC, assigned to the Lily Transportation—Toyota Dedicated route in San Ramon, California, at a regular hourly rate of $33.35 and a premium rate of $50.03. The Centerline Wage Notice, attached hereto as Exhibit E, documents these terms. The suspension destroyed this career opportunity before Plaintiff could complete his first week of employment.
B. The November 1, 2024 Encounter and Unconstitutional Arrest
18. On November 1, 2024, at approximately 12:43 a.m., Plaintiff was lawfully parked on an unpaved dirt shoulder alongside Dublin Boulevard near Fallon Road in Dublin, California. Plaintiff was asleep in his parked, stationary vehicle. He had made the responsible and professional decision to pull over and rest rather than continue driving while fatigued.
19. CHP Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez and Christopher Melano approached Plaintiff’s vehicle, purportedly to conduct a “welfare check.” However, as documented in the CHP dashcam video transcript (Exhibit B), the officers’ conduct immediately revealed a criminal investigative purpose rather than a welfare concern.
20. At timestamp 00:43:28—within fourteen seconds of initial approach and before any welfare assessment was conducted—Officer Melano stated to Officer Meza-Gonzalez: “I think it’s booze.” This declaration, made before any interaction with Plaintiff and while Plaintiff remained asleep, demonstrates that the officers had adopted a criminal investigative hypothesis before conducting any welfare evaluation.
21. The officers then conducted a warrantless entry into and search of Plaintiff’s vehicle while he remained asleep inside. The dashcam transcript reveals an approximately eleven-minute gap (from 00:46:03 to 00:57:08) during which the officers searched the vehicle without Plaintiff’s knowledge or consent. When Plaintiff was finally awakened and the encounter moved to an on-camera investigative phase, the officers subjected him to a battery of field sobriety tests despite never having observed him operate or exercise volitional movement of the vehicle.
22. The dashcam transcript further reveals an objective, audio-recorded contradiction of the officers’ sworn DS-367 statement. The officers initially claimed to have detected an odor of alcohol. However, as captured on audio, the officers discovered on scene that the open container they observed in the vehicle contained urine, not alcohol. Despite this on-scene discovery—which objectively contradicted the stated basis for the investigation—the officers proceeded to arrest Plaintiff for DUI.
23. The arrest explicitly violated the volitional movement requirement established by the California Supreme Court in Mercer v. Department of Motor Vehicles, 53 Cal.3d 916 (1991). Under Mercer, a warrantless misdemeanor DUI arrest requires the officer to have observed volitional movement of the vehicle. Because Plaintiff’s vehicle was stationary, parked, and off the roadway on an unpaved dirt shoulder, and because Plaintiff was asleep at the time of contact, no volitional movement was observed or could have been observed. The CVC § 40300.5 “obstruction of a roadway” exception was entirely inapplicable.
C. The Formal Nullification of the Arrest
24. On November 5, 2024—four days after the encounter and eleven weeks before the DMV hearing—the CHP Dublin Area Office issued a formal Detention Certificate under California Penal Code § 849(b)(1) in CHP Case No. RJ68845. The Certificate is attached hereto as Exhibit A.
25. The Detention Certificate formally certifies that there were “insufficient grounds” for a criminal complaint. By statutory mandate of Penal Code § 849(c), once such a certificate issues, the encounter “shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention only.”
26. This statutory language is mandatory, not discretionary. The Legislature’s use of “shall” leaves no room for the DMV to treat the encounter as an arrest for any purpose. The certificate did not merely decline to prosecute—it retroactively reclassified the legal character of the encounter as a matter of state law.
27. No criminal charges were ever filed against Plaintiff in connection with the November 1, 2024 encounter. The APS framework requires a lawful arrest as a jurisdictional predicate. That predicate no longer existed.
D. The Structural Collision: APS Jurisdiction Requires an Arrest That No Longer Exists
28. The APS implied consent framework under California Vehicle Code §§ 13353 and 13353.2 authorizes the DMV to suspend a driver’s license for refusal of a chemical test only upon a threshold finding that the driver was “lawfully arrested.” This is a jurisdictional predicate—without it, the DMV lacks statutory authority to sustain the suspension.
29. Three mandatory legal rules collide in this case to create an irreconcilable structural contradiction:
First, APS suspension requires a lawful arrest. California Vehicle Code §§ 13353/13353.2 explicitly condition the DMV’s authority to suspend on a finding that the driver was “lawfully arrested.”
Second, the CHP’s Detention Certificate legally erased the arrest. Under Penal Code § 849(c), once the certificate issued, the arrest “shall not be deemed an arrest, but a detention only.” This is a mandatory statutory reclassification, not a discretionary determination.
Third, the DMV imposed a suspension anyway. Despite the State’s own formal admission that the arrest predicate did not exist, Defendant Candelaria sustained the suspension as though the arrest remained legally operative.
30. This structural collision is not merely an error in fact-finding. It raises a fundamental question of federal constitutional law: Can the DMV sustain a license suspension based on an arrest that the arresting agency has already formally nullified under state law? If the answer is no, the constitutional deficiency is systemic—affecting every APS case in which the arresting agency has issued a Penal Code § 849(b)(1) Detention Certificate.
E. The Unconstitutional APS Hearing
31. On January 24, 2025, Defendant Candelaria presided over Plaintiff’s APS hearing, conducted remotely via Microsoft Teams. During the hearing, Candelaria operated under the structurally biased framework condemned by the California Court of Appeal, serving simultaneously as the prosecuting advocate for the DMV and the ostensible adjudicator of fact.
32. As the DMV’s advocate, Candelaria unilaterally introduced the DS-367 Officer’s Statement into evidence, established the State’s case, and defended the officer’s subjective articulation of probable cause against Plaintiff’s robust factual challenges. She then immediately shifted to her role as adjudicator to rule that her own advocacy was persuasive and that Plaintiff’s defense was “unpersuasive.”
33. Plaintiff presented the following evidence and arguments at the hearing, all of which Candelaria dismissed, ignored, or failed to address:
(a) The Detention Certificate under Penal Code § 849(b)(1)—a formal state instrument certifying the arrest lacked sufficient grounds—which Candelaria entirely failed to address or acknowledge in her written decision;
(b) The CHP dashcam video transcript objectively contradicting the officer’s sworn DS-367 on material facts, including the officers’ on-scene discovery that the suspected open container held urine, not alcohol;
(c) Binding California Supreme Court precedent (Mercer v. DMV) establishing that a warrantless misdemeanor DUI arrest of a person in a stationary, parked vehicle without observed volitional movement is unlawful;
(d) The absence of any criminal charges arising from the encounter.
34. Candelaria’s February 11, 2025 Notification of Findings and Decision (Exhibit C) reveals deliberate indifference to the evidence and law presented. Candelaria characterized Plaintiff’s arguments as “unpersuasive” without providing any reasoned analysis explaining why the Detention Certificate, dashcam contradictions, or Mercer precedent were unpersuasive. She applied an irrebuttable presumption of official regularity to the officer’s DS-367 sworn statement to override objective, audio-recorded contrary evidence.
35. Most critically, Candelaria explicitly endorsed the unconstitutional police conduct, ruling that the officer “would have been negligent in his job duties if he did not conduct an investigation.” This language is the language of advocacy—defending the officer’s actions—not the language of neutral adjudication.
36. Candelaria was presented with incontrovertible, objective proof that the officer’s sworn DS-367 statement contained materially false claims—specifically, the assertion of an alcohol odor that the dashcam reveals was contradicted by the on-scene discovery. Rather than evaluating this contradiction as a neutral adjudicator, Candelaria chose to ratify the false sworn statement as the basis for sustaining the suspension. This knowing endorsement of demonstrably false testimony is conduct that no reasonable hearing officer could have believed was lawful.
F. The Statewide Structural Bias: Dual Advocate-Adjudicator Framework
37. The structural bias infecting Plaintiff’s hearing is not an isolated occurrence. It is a systemic, daily feature of the DMV’s statewide APS hearing framework, operating under Director Gordon’s supervision.
38. In California DUI Lawyers Ass’n v. DMV (2022) 77 Cal.App.5th 517, the California Court of Appeal ruled that the DMV’s practice of requiring hearing officers to simultaneously serve as both the prosecuting advocate for the DMV and the trier of fact violates procedural due process. The court held that this dual role prevents the hearing officer from acting as an impartial magistrate, creating an intolerable structural bias.
39. In Knudsen v. DMV (2024) 101 Cal.App.5th 186, the Court of Appeal reaffirmed this holding and identified the constitutionally impermissible merging of prosecutorial and adjudicative functions within a single decisionmaker.
40. Despite these binding appellate decisions, the DMV continues to conduct APS hearings under the condemned dual-role framework. Every APS hearing conducted under this structure subjects the driver to the identical constitutional violation Plaintiff suffered. This is a policy and practice implemented and maintained under Director Gordon’s authority.
G. The Irrebuttable Presumption of Official Regularity as Unconstitutional Policy
41. Candelaria’s decision reveals a further systemic deficiency: the DMV’s application of an irrebuttable presumption of official regularity to police officer statements, even when those statements are objectively contradicted by audio-visual evidence.
42. In this case, the CHP dashcam transcript—an official state recording—directly contradicted the officer’s sworn DS-367 on material facts. Rather than weigh the conflicting evidence as a neutral adjudicator, Candelaria treated the DS-367 as conclusive, applying the presumption of regularity to immunize the officer’s account from challenge. This transforms what should be a rebuttable evidentiary presumption into an irrebuttable rule that guarantees the State prevails regardless of the evidence.
43. If this is the DMV’s statewide evidentiary practice—as Candelaria’s decision suggests—it raises a systemic due process concern: no driver can receive a constitutionally adequate hearing if the State’s evidence is treated as conclusive regardless of what contrary evidence the driver presents.
H. Damages
44. The suspension of Plaintiff’s CDL, effective February 20, 2025 through February 19, 2026, immediately and completely terminated Plaintiff’s employment and extinguished his capacity to earn a living as a commercial truck driver.
45. Plaintiff’s damages are concrete, documented, and severe:
(a) Lost regular wages at $33.35 per hour for standard shifts lost since the effective date of suspension, as documented in the Centerline Wage Notice (Exhibit E);
(b) Lost premium wages at $50.03 per hour for premium/overtime shifts lost since the effective date of suspension;
(c) Out-of-pocket expenses, including costs incurred for the $125.00 reissue fee, SR-22 proof of financial responsibility costs, alternative transportation, and administrative expenses;
(d) Emotional distress, humiliation, and mental anguish caused by the arbitrary and unconstitutional destruction of Plaintiff’s livelihood and professional reputation, compensable under Carey v. Piphus, 435 U.S. 247 (1978);
(e) Consequential economic damages, including damage to Plaintiff’s commercial driving record and future employability in the trucking industry.
46. The financial devastation is magnified by its timing. The suspension destroyed a career opportunity that Plaintiff had secured just two days before the encounter. The longer the unconstitutional suspension persists, the greater Plaintiff’s damages accumulate—providing both Defendants with a strong incentive to resolve this matter expeditiously.
CAUSES OF ACTION
COUNT I
42 U.S.C. § 1983 — FOURTEENTH AMENDMENT PROCEDURAL DUE PROCESS
(Against Defendant Candelaria in Her Individual Capacity)
47. Plaintiff incorporates by reference each and every allegation in the preceding paragraphs as if fully set forth herein.
48. Plaintiff’s Class A CDL constitutes a protected property interest under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Bell v. Burson, 402 U.S. 535, 539 (1971); Mackey v. Montrym, 443 U.S. 1, 10–11 (1979).
49. Defendant Candelaria, acting under color of state law, deprived Plaintiff of this protected property interest without adequate procedural due process in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
50. Candelaria’s deprivation of Plaintiff’s due process rights was accomplished through multiple, independently sufficient constitutional violations:
(a) Jurisdictional Nullity: Candelaria sustained a suspension based on an arrest that had been formally nullified by the arresting agency’s own Detention Certificate under Penal Code § 849(b)(1), thereby exercising adjudicative power over a matter where the statutory predicate—“lawful arrest”—no longer existed as a matter of law;
(b) Structural Bias: Candelaria presided over the hearing within a framework requiring her to simultaneously serve as the DMV’s prosecuting advocate and the trier of fact—a dual role explicitly condemned as a due process violation in California DUI Lawyers Ass’n v. DMV and Knudsen v. DMV;
(c) Deliberate Indifference to Exculpatory Evidence: Candelaria entirely failed to address the Detention Certificate, dismissed the dashcam contradictions without analysis, ignored binding Mercer precedent, and ratified demonstrably false sworn testimony;
(d) Irrebuttable Presumption: Candelaria applied an irrebuttable presumption of official regularity to the officer’s sworn statement, shielding the State’s case from any meaningful challenge regardless of the objective evidence presented.
51. Under the balancing test established in Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976), the deprivation was constitutionally intolerable: (1) Plaintiff’s private interest—his sole source of income—was exceptionally high; (2) the risk of erroneous deprivation was absolute when the adjudicator ignored legally binding documents and objective evidence; and (3) the government had zero legitimate interest in sustaining a suspension based on an arrest that its own agencies had formally repudiated.
52. As a direct and proximate result of Candelaria’s unconstitutional conduct, Plaintiff has suffered and continues to suffer compensatory damages, including lost wages, out-of-pocket expenses, emotional distress, and consequential economic harm.
53. Candelaria’s conduct was motivated by reckless and callous indifference to Plaintiff’s federally protected constitutional rights, warranting an award of punitive damages pursuant to Smith v. Wade, 461 U.S. 30 (1983). Candelaria knowingly sustained a suspension based on an arrest formally nullified by a Detention Certificate, knowingly ratified demonstrably false sworn testimony contradicted by objective audio-visual evidence, actively ignored binding appellate precedent, and participated in a hearing structure already declared unconstitutional by the California Court of Appeal.
COUNT II
42 U.S.C. § 1983 — DECLARATORY RELIEF
(Against Defendant Gordon in His Official Capacity)
54. Plaintiff incorporates by reference each and every allegation in the preceding paragraphs as if fully set forth herein.
55. An actual, justiciable controversy exists between the parties regarding whether the APS hearing conducted on January 24, 2025, and the resulting Notification of Findings and Decision dated February 11, 2025, violated Plaintiff’s procedural due process rights under the Fourteenth Amendment.
56. Pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §§ 2201 and 2202, Plaintiff seeks a declaratory judgment that:
(a) The APS hearing as conducted violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment because the hearing officer served simultaneously as the DMV’s prosecuting advocate and the trier of fact, creating an unconstitutional structural bias;
(b) The DMV lacked statutory authority to sustain the license suspension because the “lawful arrest” predicate required by Vehicle Code §§ 13353 and 13353.2 was destroyed by the Penal Code § 849(b)(1) Detention Certificate;
(c) The DMV’s application of an irrebuttable presumption of official regularity to override objective contrary evidence violates procedural due process.
57. This declaratory relief is sought against Director Gordon in his official capacity under the Ex parte Young doctrine. The ongoing suspension constitutes a continuing violation of federal law, authorizing prospective equitable relief notwithstanding the Eleventh Amendment.
COUNT III
42 U.S.C. § 1983 — INJUNCTIVE RELIEF
(Against Defendant Gordon in His Official Capacity — Ex parte Young)
58. Plaintiff incorporates by reference each and every allegation in the preceding paragraphs as if fully set forth herein.
59. The suspension of Plaintiff’s CDL constitutes an ongoing deprivation of a constitutionally protected property interest. Each day the suspension remains in effect, Plaintiff suffers continuing harm: he is barred from his profession, denied his primary source of income, and subjected to an ongoing constitutional violation. This continuing deprivation satisfies the Ex parte Young requirement of an “ongoing violation of federal law.”
60. Plaintiff seeks injunctive relief against Director Gordon in his official capacity, including:
(a) An order vacating the February 11, 2025 Notification of Findings and Decision in APS Case No. 34739340;
(b) An order directing the immediate reinstatement of Plaintiff’s Class A CDL, free of the penalties imposed by the unconstitutional suspension;
(c) An order prohibiting the DMV from imposing the $125.00 reissue fee and the SR-22 proof of financial responsibility requirement stemming from the unconstitutional suspension;
(d) An order requiring that any new hearing, if one is conducted, be held before a neutral decisionmaker who does not simultaneously serve as the DMV’s prosecuting advocate.
61. Plaintiff has no adequate remedy at law for the ongoing deprivation. Each day of suspension causes irreparable economic and professional harm. The balance of equities favors Plaintiff, as the State has no legitimate interest in maintaining a suspension based on an arrest it has formally repudiated. The public interest is served by ensuring that state administrative agencies comply with constitutional due process requirements.
PRAYER FOR RELIEF
WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court enter judgment in his favor and against Defendants as follows:
As to Defendant Candelaria (Individual Capacity):
A. Compensatory damages in an amount to be proven at trial, including but not limited to lost wages, lost earning capacity, consequential economic damages, and damages for emotional distress, humiliation, and mental anguish;
B. Punitive damages in an amount sufficient to punish Defendant Candelaria’s willful and reckless disregard for Plaintiff’s constitutional rights and to deter similar conduct in the future, pursuant to Smith v. Wade, 461 U.S. 30 (1983), and as warranted by Defendant’s deliberate indifference to Plaintiff’s clearly established rights;
As to Defendant Gordon (Official Capacity):
C. A declaratory judgment that the APS hearing conducted on January 24, 2025, and the resulting Notification of Findings and Decision dated February 11, 2025, violated Plaintiff’s procedural due process rights under the Fourteenth Amendment;
D. A declaratory judgment that the DMV lacks statutory authority to sustain a license suspension when the “lawful arrest” predicate has been destroyed by the arresting agency’s issuance of a Penal Code § 849(b)(1) Detention Certificate;
E. A permanent injunction vacating the February 11, 2025 Order of Suspension and directing the immediate reinstatement of Plaintiff’s Class A CDL, free of all penalties imposed by the unconstitutional suspension, including the $125.00 reissue fee and the SR-22 proof of financial responsibility requirement;
F. An injunction requiring that any new hearing, if one is conducted, be held before a neutral decisionmaker who does not simultaneously serve as the DMV’s prosecuting advocate;
As to All Defendants:
G. Reasonable attorney’s fees and costs pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 1988, to the extent applicable;
H. Pre-judgment and post-judgment interest as permitted by law;
I. Such other and further relief as this Court deems just, equitable, and proper.
DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL
68. Plaintiff demands a trial by jury on all claims and issues so triable pursuant to the Seventh Amendment to the United States Constitution and Rule 38 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

AGAINST ALPINE TRUCK SALES, INC.
I, BRENDAN NGWA NFORBI, declare:
I. PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
1. I am the Plaintiff in the above-entitled action and am over eighteen years of age. The

Declaration in support of my Request for Entry of Default Judgment by the Court (Judicial
Council Form CIV-100) against Defendant ALPINE TRUCK SALES, INC. ("Alpine"), pursuant
to Code of Civil Procedure section 585, subdivision (b), and California Rules of Court, rule
3.1800.
2. This Declaration is submitted together with the following companion documents
constituting my prove-up package as to Alpine: (a) Plaintiff's Request for Entry of Default and
Court Judgment (Form CIV-100); (b) this Declaration; and (c) the exhibits attached hereto, which
are the same documentary exhibits previously submitted in support of the default judgment
prove-up against co-defendant Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. ("Diamond"), attached again here so
that this filing is complete and self-contained as to Alpine.
II. PROCEDURAL POSTURE
3. The operative pleading in this action is the First Amended Complaint ("FAC"), which
names Alpine as a defendant on the theory that Alpine is Diamond's successor in interest, mere
continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or a participant in a fraudulent transfer under
the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act (Civ. Code section 3439 et seq.).
4. Alpine was personally served with the Amended Summons, the First Amended
Complaint, and the Notice of Case Assignment and Notice of Hearing on July 1, 2026, at 9:00
a.m., by delivery to Mustaqem Usmani, Manager, at 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California
95380, by San Joaquin County Sheriff's Deputy T. Caldwell, under Code of Civil Procedure
section 416.10. Proof of Service (Form POS-010, Levying Officer File No. 2026002577) was
signed July 2, 2026 by the Sheriff's Authorized Agent and is on file with this Court.

5. Alpine's deadline to respond to the FAC expired thirty (30) days after service, on July
31, 2026. Alpine filed no responsive pleading, demurrer, or other appearance, and no
meet-and-confer contact was received from Alpine at any time before or after that deadline. I
have submitted a Request for Entry of Default (Form CIV-100) against Alpine, and the Court has
entered, or will shortly enter, Alpine's default as reflected in the Court's file.
6. Because Alpine has defaulted, the well-pleaded factual allegations of the FAC
concerning Alpine's liability are deemed admitted. (Steven M. Garber & Assocs. v. Eskandarian
(2007) 150 Cal.App.4th 813, 823; Kim v. Westmoore Partners, Inc. (2011) 201 Cal.App.4th 267,
281.) The well-pleaded allegations include, without limitation: that Diamond rebranded to Alpine
during the pendency of this action; that Alpine has operated from the same locations as Diamond,
including 1201 S Soderquist Road, Turlock, California, under the same Osmani family ownership
and management; and that Alpine is therefore liable for Diamond's obligations in this action as its
successor in interest, mere continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or by reason of a
fraudulent transfer of Diamond's business and assets to Alpine.
7. This Declaration addresses only the amount and proof of damages as against Alpine. I
have made no effort to relitigate liability, which is deemed established by the default, nor to
relitigate the underlying fraud and misrepresentation claims against Diamond, which were proved
up separately -- and on the same exhibits reattached hereto -- in the default judgment package
previously submitted as to Diamond.
III. SUCCESSOR LIABILITY IS DERIVATIVE, NOT ADDITIONAL
8. Alpine's liability in this action is derivative of Diamond's liability. Alpine is not sued
for independently committing fraud, misrepresentation, or breach of contract in the underlying
vehicle sale transaction; rather, Alpine is sued as the entity that has, by operation of the
successor-liability and alter-ego doctrines pleaded in the FAC, become answerable for the single

9. Accordingly, Plaintiff does NOT seek, and this Declaration does NOT request, an
additional or duplicative award of damages against Alpine on top of the judgment sought against
Diamond. Plaintiff instead requests that judgment be entered against Alpine in the same total
amount requested against Diamond, on a joint and several basis, so that Plaintiff may recover the
single judgment sum from either or both defendants, without any double recovery. This is
consistent with the [Proposed] Judgment (Form JUD-100) already on file in this action, which at
item 8 expressly provides that "Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. is jointly and severally liable with
Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. as Diamond's successor, mere continuation, alter ego, and/or
fraudulent transference."
IV. DAMAGES (SAME SUM AS THE DIAMOND JUDGMENT)
10. The itemized calculation of damages is set forth in full in the Declaration in Support
of Request for Default Judgment previously filed against Diamond, and in Attachment 4b to
Plaintiff's Case Management Statement (Form CM-110) filed July 20, 2026, both of which are
incorporated herein by reference. The supporting documentary exhibits (Exhibits 1 through 10)
are attached to this Declaration for completeness. In summary: documented out-of-pocket losses
of $20,218.65; additional sworn, undocumented out-of-pocket losses of $5,750.00; conservatively
calculated lost commercial income of $23,400.00 (18 weeks x $1,300/week); and prejudgment
interest under Civil Code section 3287(a) (7%, approximately 3.04 years) of $4,302.55 -- for a
compensatory subtotal of $53,671.20.
11. Plaintiff additionally requests punitive damages of $25,000.00 under Civil Code
section 3294, based on the well-pleaded and, as to Diamond, now-admitted allegations that
Diamond's concealment of the DEF/SCR emissions defect was intentional, malicious, fraudulent,

and management; and that Alpine is therefore liable for Diamond's obligations in this action as its
successor in interest, mere continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or by reason of a
fraudulent transfer of Diamond's business and assets to Alpine.

expired on June 11, 2026. Diamond filed no responsive pleading, demurrer, or other appearance. I
have submitted a Request for Entry of Default (Form CIV-100) against Diamond, and the Court
has entered, or will shortly enter, Diamond's default as reflected in the Court's file.

WRIT OF EXECUTION OR SALE. Your rights and duties are indicated on the accompanying Notice of Levy (form EJ-150).  
 
WRIT OF POSSESSION OF PERSONAL PROPERTY. If the levying officer is not able to take custody of the property, the levying 
officer will demand that you turn over the property. If custody is not obtained following demand, the judgment may be enforced as a 
money judgment for the value of the property specified in the judgment or in a supplemental order.  
 
WRIT OF POSSESSION OF REAL PROPERTY. If the premises are not vacated within five days after the date of service on the  
occupant or, if service is by posting, within five days after service on you, the levying officer will remove the occupants from the real  
property and place the judgment creditor in possession of the property. Except for a mobile home, personal property remaining on the 
premises will be sold or otherwise disposed of in accordance with Code of Civil Procedure section 1174 unless you or the owner of the 
property pays the judgment creditor the reasonable cost of storage and takes possession of the personal property not later than 15 
days after the time the judgment creditor takes possession of the premises.  
 
EXCEPTION IF RENTAL HOUSING UNIT WAS FORECLOSED. If the residential property that you are renting was sold in a 
foreclosure, you have additional time before you must vacate the premises. If you have a lease for a fixed term, such as for a year, you 
may remain in the property until the term is up. If you have a periodic lease or tenancy, such as from month to month, you may remain 
in the property for 90 days after receiving a notice to quit. A blank Claim of Right to Possession and Notice of Hearing (form CP10) 
accompanies this writ. You may claim your right to remain on the property by filling it out and giving it to the sheriff or levying officer. 
 
EXCEPTION IF YOU WERE NOT SERVED WITH A FORM CALLED PREJUDGMENT CLAIM OF RIGHT TO POSSESSION. If you 
were not named in the judgment for possession and you occupied the premises on the date on which the unlawful detainer case was 
filed, you may object to the enforcement of the judgment against you. You must complete Claim of Right to Possession and Notice of 
Hearing (form CP10) and give it to the sheriff or levying officer. A blank form accompanies this writ. You have this right whether or not 
the property you are renting was sold in a foreclosure. 
 
JUDGMENTS FOR PERSONAL DEBT. If you are the judgment debtor identified in item 4 on this form, and if item 21 on this form says 
the judgment is for personal debt, the judgment creditor is required to verify your address before asking the levying officer to enforce 
this Writ of Execution. The judgment creditor must give the levying officer a completed copy of Declaration of Address Verification 
(form WG-015/EJ-135) and must file completed form WG-015/EJ-135 with the court within 10 business days of giving a copy of the 
form to the levying officer. If the judgment creditor doesn't take these steps, you can ask the court to stay any wage garnishment order, 
bank account levy, or other levy related to this Writ of Execution. You can use Application for Stay of Levy or Garnishment (form 
WG-017/EJ-137) to ask the court to stay the levy or garnishment until the address verification has been completed.

days after the time the judgment creditor takes possession of the premises.  
 
EXCEPTION IF RENTAL HOUSING UNIT WAS FORECLOSED. If the residential property that you are renting was sold in a 
foreclosure, you have additional time before you must vacate the premises. If you have a lease for a fixed term, such as for a year, you 
may remain in the property until the term is up. If you have a periodic lease or tenancy, such as from month to month, you may remain 
in the property for 90 days after receiving a notice to quit. A blank Claim of Right to Possession and Notice of Hearing (form CP10) 
accompanies this writ. You may claim your right to remain on the property by filling it out and giving it to the sheriff or levying officer.

Hearing (form CP10) and give it to the sheriff or levying officer. A blank form accompanies this writ. You have this right whether or not 
the property you are renting was sold in a foreclosure.

successor in interest, mere continuation, de facto merger, and/or alter ego, and/or by reason of a
fraudulent transfer of Diamond's business and assets to Alpine.

have made no effort to relitigate liability, which is deemed established by the default, nor to
relitigate the underlying fraud and misrepresentation claims against Diamond, which were proved
up separately -- and on the same exhibits reattached hereto -- in the default judgment package
previously submitted as to Diamond.

Brief Statement of the Case (CM-110, Item 4b):
On or about April 4, 2023, Plaintiff Brendan Ngwa Nforbi purchased a 2014 Volvo VNL diesel
semi-truck, VIN 4V4NC9EH6EN142206, from Defendant Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. for a total
price of $27,092.75, including a deposit of $12,345.10. Diamond knowingly concealed a material
defect in the truck's Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) and Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR)
emissions systems, rendering the truck non-compliant with California emissions law and unfit
for the lawful commercial highway operation for which it was purchased.
Shortly after purchase, the truck experienced engine derate (limp mode), emitted excessive
black smoke, and lost the ability to exceed approximately 35 mph, rendering it commercially
useless. The defect was pre-existing and known to Diamond through the prior owner's disclosure.
Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. is sued as Diamond's successor in interest, mere continuation, de facto
merger, alter ego, and/or as a participant in a fraudulent transfer under the Uniform Voidable
Transactions Act (Civ. Code 3439 et seq.). Diamond rebranded to Alpine during the pendency
of this action, operating from the same locations with the same Osmani family ownership.

II.  PROCEDURAL POSTURE
3. The operative pleading in this action is the First Amended Complaint ("FAC"), which
asserts eight causes of action against Defendant Diamond: (1) Fraudulent Concealment; (2)
Intentional Misrepresentation; (3) Negligent Misrepresentation; (4) Breach of Contract; (5)
Breach of Implied Warranty of Merchantability (Cal. Comm. Code section 2314); (6) Violation of
the Unfair Competition Law (Bus. & Prof. Code section 17200 et seq.); (7) Rescission and
Restitution; and (8) Declaratory Relief.
4. The FAC was personally served on Diamond on May 12, 2026, and the Proof of
Service was filed with this Court on May 18, 2026. Diamond's deadline to respond to the FAC
expired on June 11, 2026. Diamond filed no responsive pleading, demurrer, or other appearance. I
have submitted a Request for Entry of Default (Form CIV-100) against Diamond, and the Court
has entered, or will shortly enter, Diamond's default as reflected in the Court's file.
5. Because Diamond has defaulted, the well-pleaded factual allegations of the FAC
concerning liability are deemed admitted. (Steven M. Garber & Assocs. v. Eskandarian (2007)

The well-pleaded allegations include, without limitation: that Diamond knowingly sold to me a
2014 Volvo VNL diesel semi-truck (VIN 4V4NC9EH6EN142206) that suffered from an
undisclosed and material defect in its Diesel Exhaust Fluid ("DEF") and Selective Catalytic
Reduction ("SCR") emissions systems; that the defect rendered the truck non-compliant with
California emissions law and unsafe for highway operation; that Diamond had pre-sale
knowledge of the defect and concealed it; and that Diamond's conduct was intentional, malicious,
fraudulent, and oppressive within the meaning of Civil Code section 3294.
6. This Declaration addresses only the amount and proof of damages. I have made no
effort to relitigate liability, which is deemed established by the defaults.
III.  THE TRANSACTION AND THE FAILURE

4V4NC9EH6EN142206) from Diamond. The transaction was documented by a Retail Buyer's
Order reflecting a Cash Price of $26,900.00 and Total Charges of $27,092.75 after document and
title fees. A true and correct copy of the Retail Buyer's Order is attached as Exhibit 1.
8. I paid Diamond a deposit of $12,345.10 by certified funds at the time of sale. This
amount appears in the "DEPOSIT" line and is reflected in the "TOTAL CREDITS" line of the
Retail Buyer's Order (Exh. 1, p. 1).
9. The remaining balance of $14,747.65 was financed through a third-party lender, Dakota
Financial LLC, which was selected, arranged, or facilitated by Diamond in connection with the
sale.

12. I purchased the truck specifically to use it in commercial freight service under my own

Lease-On Owner Operator Agreement with Gobbato Builders, LLC (MC #1357325) under which
I would haul freight for compensation paid weekly by Friday settlement. The Lease-On

enforce any term of, or claim any continuing benefit under, that transaction.
(b) That Diamond's conduct in connection with the sale of the subject truck
constituted unlawful, unfair, and fraudulent business acts and practices within the meaning
of California Business and Professions Code section 17200 et seq., as pleaded in the
FAC's Sixth Cause of Action.
VIII.  PREJUDGMENT INTEREST

or capable of being made certain by calculation, and the right to recover them vested on the dates
each charge was incurred. I am therefore entitled to prejudgment interest on those amounts at the

to the date of judgment, pursuant to Civil Code section 3287, subdivision (a). (See North Oakland
Medical Clinic v. Rogers (1998) 65 Cal.App.4th 824, 828-830.)

IX.  PUNITIVE DAMAGES
29. The FAC pleads, and Diamond's default admits, that Diamond's conduct was
intentional, malicious, fraudulent, and oppressive within the meaning of Civil Code section 3294.

the well-pleaded factual allegations supporting that conduct are now deemed established for
purposes of this prove-up.

Diamond's admitted fraudulent concealment and intentional misrepresentation, the
multi-jurisdictional commercial scale of Diamond's operations alleged in FAC paragraph 7, and
the post-filing rebrand from Diamond Truck Sales, Inc. to Alpine Truck Sales, Inc. alleged in the
FAC as a badge of consciousness of liability and fraudulent intent. The requested $25,000.00
figure is also well below a 1:1 ratio with the compensatory damages requested in this Declaration,

Find out if you need to pay a fee for service by asking the court’s self-help center, a lawyer, or the sheriff’s office. 
Here are some situations where you do not need to pay for service: 
If you have a fee waiver in your case (fee waiver granted by a judge on form FW-003 or FW-005). 
If you are serving a domestic violence, elder abuse, or gun violence restraining order. 
If you have a civil harassment, workplace violence, or school violence restraining order based on a credible threat of
violence or stalking.
Give this form and a copy of all the court papers you need served to the sheriff or marshal, including a copy of a fee 
waiver (if you have one). You can turn in your papers in person or send them electronically. 
You should get a form back from the sheriff. 
If the sheriff was able to serve your court papers, you should receive a form (called a proof of service). Make sure 
you get a copy from the sheriff and file it with the court. Note that if there is a court stamp at the top right corner 
of the first page, it has already been filed and you do not need to file it with the court. 
If the sheriff was unable to serve your court papers, you should receive a form (sometimes called declaration of due 
diligence) that tells you that service was unsuccessful and will give details about when the sheriff tried to serve the 
person. If the sheriff was unable to serve your papers, you can ask a lawyer or court’s self-help center about your 
next steps.
To find your local court self-help center, go to selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/. Self-help center staff will not act as your lawyer 
but may be able to give you information to help you decide what to do in your case. Services are free.

non-discretionary duties owed to Petitioner under California Penal Code section 679.10 (as
amended by AB 1261, Stats. 2023, ch. 679, eff. Jan. 1, 2024). The duties at issue are the duties of
a state law-enforcement "certifying entity" and "certifying official" to: (a) certify a Form I-918,

own custody, and nowhere reconciles its conclusion with CHP's own prior section 851.6

incident "does not meet the standard of qualifying criminal activity identified in Section 679.10 of
the California Penal Code," "does not meet the standards of the Immigration and Nationality Act
Section 101(a)(15)(U)(iii)," and "found no substantially similar qualifying criminal activity as
defined in Section 679.10(d) PC."

perjury. CHP's own contemporaneous documentary record—the dashcam audio-video recording,
the arrest report, and the section 851.6 detention certificate—establishes these offenses on its

helpfulness; (c) compel Respondents to comply with the reason-giving requirement imposed by

First, CHP's own dashcam audio-video recording (Exhibit 5) contradicts
CHP's own sworn arrest report (Exhibit 6) on four discrete material points—the

reclassified the arrest as "a detention only, not an arrest" for "insufficient grounds

determination, four days after the incident, that the restraint was without legal

Third, Penal Code section 679.10(h) creates a rebuttable presumption of
victim helpfulness when the victim has not refused or failed to provide reasonably

8. The relief sought is targeted and modest: vacate the conclusory denial; require

comply with the written-reasons mandate of section 679.10(g). This Petition does not ask this

STATUTORY AND LEGAL FRAMEWORK
A. Ordinary Writ of Mandate Under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1085
18. Code of Civil Procedure section 1085 authorizes the issuance of a writ of mandate by
any court "to any inferior tribunal, corporation, board, or person, to compel the performance of an
act which the law specially enjoins, as a duty resulting from an office, trust, or station." The
traditional elements are: (a) a clear, present, and ministerial duty in the respondent; (b) a clear,
present, and beneficial right in the petitioner to performance of that duty; and (c) the absence of a
plain, speedy, and adequate alternative remedy in the ordinary course of law.
19. "Shall" creates a ministerial duty enforceable by writ. A statutory directive in
mandatory form imposes a ministerial duty, the breach of which is enforceable by writ. (See Gov.
Code § 14 ["shall" is mandatory, "may" is permissive]; Haggis v. City of Los Angeles (2000) 22
Cal.4th 490, 498-499 ["shall" is ordinarily mandatory for purposes of Government Code section
815.6]; Common Cause v. Board of Supervisors (1989) 49 Cal.3d 432, 443 ["shall" creates a

20. Mandate lies to correct abuse of discretion. Although a court will not substitute its
judgment for an agency's on a purely discretionary decision, mandate lies (a) to compel an agency
to exercise its discretion at all where it has refused to do so; (b) to compel an agency to apply the
correct legal standard; and (c) to set aside a decision that reflects a failure to proceed in the
manner required by law, or that is arbitrary, capricious, or wholly unsupported by the record. (See
Saleeby v. State Bar (1985) 39 Cal.3d 547, 562 [in traditional mandamus, court determines
whether agency action was arbitrary, capricious, or without evidentiary support, and whether it
failed to conform to the law]; Carloss v. County of Alameda (2015) 242 Cal.App.4th 116
[decision is abuse of discretion if arbitrary, capricious, entirely lacking in evidentiary support, or
without reasonable or rational basis as a matter of law]; SN Sands Corp. v. City and County of
San Francisco (2008) 167 Cal.App.4th 185, 189 [same]; Western/California, Ltd. v. Dry Creek
Joint Elementary Sch. Dist. (1996) 50 Cal.App.4th 1461, 1496-1497 [same]; Bunnett v. Regents
of University of California (1995) 35 Cal.App.4th 843, 848.)
21. An agency decision that ignores the agency's own contrary evidence and prior
determinations is arbitrary and capricious as a matter of law. A decision is arbitrary and
capricious if it fails to address relevant evidence, fails to articulate a rational connection between
the facts found and the decision made, or is so devoid of factual support as to be irrational. A
decision that ignores the agency's own exculpatory evidence and contradicts the agency's own
prior contemporaneous determinations is, by definition, both arbitrary and contrary to the
substantial-evidence rule under section 1085.

26. Mandatory certification. Section 679.10 directs that, upon request of a victim of
qualifying criminal activity, a certifying entity "shall" complete and certify Form I-918,
Supplement B when the statutory elements are met. The Legislature's use of "shall" imposes a
mandatory, ministerial duty enforceable by writ of mandate. (Haggis, supra, 22 Cal.4th at pp.
498-499; Common Cause, supra, 49 Cal.3d at p. 443.)
27. Rebuttable presumption of helpfulness (subdivision (h)). Section 679.10(h) creates
a "rebuttable presumption that the victim is helpful, has been helpful, or is likely to be helpful" in
the detection, investigation, or prosecution of the qualifying criminal activity if the victim has not
refused or failed to provide information and assistance reasonably requested by the certifying
entity. The presumption operates against the certifying entity and may be overcome only by
evidence of refusal or failure to cooperate. An agency that fails to apply a controlling statutory
presumption commits legal error reviewable by mandamus.
28. Thirty-day processing deadline (subdivision (j)). Section 679.10(j) requires that a
certifying entity "shall process" a Form I-918, Supplement B certification request within 30 days
of the request, with shorter deadlines in specified circumstances.
29. No prosecution required (subdivision (k)). Section 679.10(k) provides that "[a]
current investigation, the filing of charges, closing of a case, and a prosecution or conviction are
not required for the victim to request and obtain the Form I-918 Supplement B certification."
Whether a prosecution has occurred is therefore legally irrelevant to the certification
determination, and any denial that rests, expressly or implicitly, on the absence of charges or
prosecution is contrary to law.
30. Reason-giving requirement (subdivision (g)) — AB 1261's central procedural
reform. Section 679.10(g), as amended by AB 1261, requires that a certifying entity that does not

The Legislature expressly imposed a procedural duty of meaningful explanation precisely to
forestall conclusory, pro-forma, or boilerplate refusals that frustrate both the requester's ability to
understand the basis for denial and any reviewing court's ability to evaluate the agency's
reasoning. The duty to provide written, specific reasons is itself ministerial: it does not depend on

31. Limited grounds for withdrawal (subdivision (l)). A certifying official may
withdraw a certification only if the victim refuses to provide information and assistance
reasonably requested. No comparable cabining provision exists for an initial denial precisely
because the Legislature anticipated that the presumption of helpfulness and the reason-giving
requirement together would constrain denial discretion.

Bulletins (most recently DLE-2024-05) instructing all state and local law enforcement
agencies—including CHP—that under AB 1261 they "shall process" certification requests within
the statutory timeline; that the rebuttable presumption of helpfulness applies; that no prosecution
is required; that the reason-giving requirement is a substantive procedural obligation that
conclusory letters do not satisfy; and that certification shall not be denied on grounds such as the
victim's criminal record, immigration history, or the absence of filed charges. The Attorney
General's interpretation of section 679.10 is entitled to substantial weight.

A. The Government Claims Act Does Not Apply
65. The Government Claims Act (Gov. Code, § 810 et seq.) governs claims "for money or

It seeks only a peremptory writ of mandate vacating an unlawful denial, an order compelling
lawful reconsideration, and declaratory relief concerning the parties' rights under Penal Code
section 679.10. Equitable relief of this kind is not subject to the Act's claim-presentation
requirement. (See Loehr v. Ventura County Community College Dist. (1983) 147 Cal.App.3d
1071, 1080-1081 [claims for relief other than damages not subject to Government Claims Act];

procedure, and no other agency-level mechanism by which a denial of certification may be

because USCIS lacks any authority to certify or to compel a state certifying entity to do so;
without a properly executed Form I-918, Supplement B, a U-visa petition cannot be filed.

I.
CALIFORNIA LAW MANDATES CERTIFICATION

California Penal Code § 679.10 imposes affirmative, non-discretionary obligations on state 
law enforcement agencies—including CHP—to process U visa certification requests. Specifically:
Mandatory Processing: Under § 679.10(j), a certifying entity “shall process a Form I-918 
Supplement B certification within 30 days of request.” This is not a discretionary guideline; 
it is a legislative mandate.
Rebuttable Presumption of Helpfulness: Under § 679.10(h), there is a “rebuttable 
presumption that the victim is helpful, has been helpful, or is likely to be helpful” if the 
victim has not refused or failed to provide information and assistance reasonably requested 
by law enforcement. I have not refused any such request. To the contrary, I have 
affirmatively cooperated at every stage.
No Prosecution Required: Under § 679.10(k), “a current investigation, the filing of 
charges, closing of a case, and a prosecution or conviction are not required for the victim to 
request and obtain the Form I-918 Supplement B certification.” The CHP’s investigation 
need not be complete—nor need it result in prosecution—for the certification to issue.
Limited Grounds for Withdrawal: Under § 679.10(l), a certifying official “may only 
withdraw the certification if the victim refuses to provide information and assistance when 
reasonably requested.” No such refusal has occurred here.
The California Attorney General’s Information Bulletin No. DLE-2024-05, issued to all 
state and local law enforcement agencies, reaffirms these obligations and encourages agencies to 
“be vigilant in identifying and supporting immigrant crime victims who may be eligible for U 
visas.”
II.
THE STATUTORY ELEMENTS ARE SATISFIED
To obtain a U visa certification, three elements must be established: (1) the petitioner is a 
victim of qualifying criminal activity; (2) the petitioner possesses information concerning the 
criminal activity; and (3) the petitioner has been helpful, is being helpful, or is likely to be helpful 
in the investigation or prosecution. Each element is met here.
A.
Qualifying Criminal Activity
On November 1, 2024, on Interstate 580 East in Livermore, Alameda County, CHP 
Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez (#023295) and Jose Melano (#023054) subjected me to criminal 
conduct constituting multiple qualifying offenses under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii), including:
False Imprisonment / Unlawful Criminal Restraint (Cal. Penal Code § 236)—I was 
unlawfully arrested, handcuffed, and detained; the arrest was subsequently reclassified 
as a “detention” in a revised report, an implicit acknowledgment that the initial restraint 
was without legal justification;
Felonious Assault / Battery (Cal. Penal Code § 242)—an involuntary blood draw was 
performed on my person based on a misrepresented warrant, constituting an unlawful 
application of force;

Obstruction of Justice (analogous to Cal. Penal Code §§ 118, 182)—the officers 
fabricated sworn arrest reports that are directly contradicted by the CHP’s own 
dashcam recording, constituting the creation of false evidence under penalty of perjury; 
and
Perjury (Cal. Penal Code § 118)—false statements in sworn reports contradicted by 
objective dashcam evidence.
Each of these offenses is independently enumerated as qualifying criminal activity under 
the VTVPA. The dashcam transcript—objective, contemporaneous evidence in CHP’s own 
custody—corroborates these allegations and directly contradicts the officers’ written reports.
B.
Possession of Information
As the direct victim and sole civilian percipient witness to the November 1, 2024 incident, I 
possess firsthand information regarding every aspect of the qualifying criminal activity. I have 
gathered and preserved key evidence, including the dashcam transcript, the arrest report, and the 
certificate of detention—all of which I have made available to CHP through this complaint process.
C.
Helpfulness
I have been helpful, am currently being helpful, and am likely to continue being helpful in 
the investigation of this criminal activity. My cooperation includes: filing the citizen complaint that 
initiated this investigation (File No. 390.18437.17620); filing a separate complaint with the 
Commission on Peace Officer Standards and Training (POST Case No. PUBLIC-26-000371); 
participating in DMV administrative proceedings related to the incident; gathering and preserving 
the dashcam transcript as objective evidence; and presenting all evidence to CHP and related 
agencies. At no time have I refused or failed to provide information or assistance reasonably 
requested by any investigating entity.
Under § 679.10(h), these facts create a rebuttable presumption of helpfulness that can only 
be overcome by evidence that I have refused to cooperate. No such evidence exists.
III.
SUBSTANTIAL PHYSICAL AND MENTAL ABUSE
I have suffered substantial physical and mental abuse as a direct result of the qualifying

IV.
IMPORTANT CLARIFICATIONS FOR THE CERTIFYING OFFICIAL
I respectfully call your attention to several points the Department of Homeland Security 
and the California Attorney General have emphasized for certifying officials:

Signing the certification does not grant a visa. The Form I-918 Supplement B is not a 
visa approval. It is a factual certification that the individual is or was a victim of qualifying 
criminal activity and has been helpful. USCIS independently adjudicates the visa petition, 
conducts a full background check, and makes all eligibility determinations. The certifying 
official’s signature carries no immigration consequences standing alone.
This certification concerns the officers’ conduct, not the outcome of the complaint. 
The standard is whether the petitioner is a victim of qualifying criminal activity and has 
been helpful—not whether the investigation has concluded or discipline has been imposed. 
California law is explicit that no prosecution, conviction, or even a pending investigation is 
required.
CHP has a public-safety interest in certifying. As the DHS U Visa Law Enforcement 
Resource Guide emphasizes, certifying U visa petitions builds trust within communities, 
encourages crime reporting, and strengthens law enforcement’s ability to detect, 
investigate, and prosecute criminal activity. CHP’s cooperation here advances these goals.

TIME-SENSITIVE REQUEST AND 30-DAY STATUTORY DEADLINE

II.
SUMMARY OF THE EVIDENTIARY RECORD
The following documentary evidence has been compiled and is referenced throughout this

Exhibit A — CHP Dashcam Video Transcript. A verbatim, timestamped transcription of

criminal activity.

official certificate issued under Penal Code § 851.6, in which CHP itself retroactively 
reclassified the arrest as “a detention only, not an arrest” and certified “insufficient grounds

Exhibit D — Declaration of Brendan Ngehsi Newanforbi. A sworn declaration under

Exhibits E and F — Pay Stubs and Wage Notice (Centerline Drivers, LLC). Twenty-
six consecutive weekly pay stubs from Centerline Drivers, LLC, covering the pay periods 
from May 5, 2024 through January 3, 2025, documenting Petitioner’s earnings as a

Petitioner’s livelihood and the quantum of economic harm caused by the DMV suspension.

suspension proceedings and the restriction/disqualification of Petitioner’s Class A

Exhibit H — CHP Complaint Assignment Letter (Captain G. Serrato, March 26,

Sergeant Eric Dutra as the investigator, and CHP’s acknowledgment that the matter is
